title.narrative: Saferworld - Addressing Conflict Drivers in Uganda 2020-2024
Saferworld -Hantera konflikt och konfliktorsaker i Uganda 2020-2024

description.narrative:
Saferworld has applied to Sida for funding of 55,000,000SEK to implement a programme titled "Addressing Drivers of Conflict in Uganda." for three (3) years.
The programme which will be implemented with Saferworld's partner, Transcultural-psycho-social Organisation, aims to contribute to more peaceful, secure and resilient communities in Uganda, through working with and supporting communities, formal and informal authorities and civil society to work together to build peace and resolve conflicts.
Specifically, the programme aims to achieve three outcomes as shown below;
Outcome 1 - Communities (including women, youth, refugees, hosts and other marginalized groups) at risk of- and/or affected by conflict in at least 14 districts identify, prioritise, analyse, monitor and take coordinated action to respond to local conflict issues and their root causes, through existing and/or new community peace building structures.
Outcome 2 - Formal and informal authorities responsible for building peace, security, justice and psychosocial healing at local, district and national levels, consult more with communities on identified conflict issues, support community peace building structures in responding to conflict issues, and incorporate community concerns (including issues affecting marginalized groups) into their related responses.
Outcome 3 – Civil Society Organisations work together to influence relevant peace, security and justice processes and decision-making at district/regional and national levels, including donors and private sector, connecting them to communities’ concerns and priorities; and to incorporate conflict sensitive practices into their activities and programmes.
It will address four major conflict drivers namely natural resources, inadequate transitional justice processes, flawed electoral processes and refugee influx. It notes the interconnected and cyclic nature of conflict drivers and proposes a wide range of peacebuilding solutions at multiple levels including community, district, regional and national levels.
The programme will be implemented in 14 districts across four sub-regions in Uganda namely; Lamwo, Amuru and Nwoya in northern Uganda; Yumbe, Adjumani, Arua and Moyo in West Nile; Moroto, Nakapiripit, Kaabong and Amudat in Karamoja; Kasese, Buliisa and Hoima in Western Uganda/Rwenzori region. The primary criteria for the selection of the 14 districts is the presence of unaddressed multiple and interlinked conflict drivers.

Saferworld har ansökt till Sida om finansierng om 55 000 000 sek för att genomföra ett 3-årigt program med titeln ”Adressing conflict drivers in Uganda 2020-2023”.
Programmet som Saferworld kommer att genomföra tillsammans med deras partner Transcultural-psycho-social Organisation (TPO) syftar till att bidra till mer fredliga, säkra och motståndskraftiga samhällen i Uganda. De kommer att samverka med olika samhällsstrukturer och -grupper, formella och informella beslutandestrukturer och det civila samhället för att söka lösa konflikter och bygga fred.
Specifikt syftar programmet till att uppnå tre resultat (outcomes) enligt nedan;
1 – riskutsatta grupper (inklusive kvinnor, ungdomar, flyktingar, värdar och andra marginaliserade grupper) i minst 14 distrikt som kan påverkas av konflikt ska identifiera, prioritera, analysera, övervaka och vidta samordnade åtgärder för att bemöta lokala konflikter och deras bakomliggande orsaker, genom antingen befintliga eller nya fredsbyggande strukturer.
2 - Formella och informella myndigheter som ansvarar för att bygga fred, säkerhet, rättvisa och psykosocial läkning på lokal, distrikts- och nationell nivå, ska samråda mer med lokalsamhällen om identifierade konfliktfrågor, stödja samhällsstrukturer för fredsbyggande när det gäller att bemöta konflikter och införliva de samhällsfrågor som påverkar riskutsatta och marginaliserade grupper i deras respons.
3 – Civilsamhällesorganisationer samarbetar för att påverka relevanta processer för fred, säkerhet och rättvisa och beslutsfattande på distrikts-, regional och nationell nivå (även inkluderat givare och den privata sektorn), och kopplar dem till lokalsamhällens problem och prioriteringar, och för att inlemma konfliktkänsliga arbetsmetoder i sin verksamhet och sina program.
Programmet kommer att ta upp fyra viktiga konfliktorsaker nämligen naturresurser, otillräcklig övergångsrättvisa, bristfälliga valprocesser och flyktingtillströmning. I programmet tas hänsyn till konfliktorsakernas sammankopplade och cykliska karaktär och man föreslår ett brett spektrum av fredsbyggande lösningar på flera nivåer, samhälls-, distrikts-, regional- och nationsnivå.
Programmet kommer att genomföras i 14 distrikt i fyra delregioner i Uganda nämligen; Lamwo, Amuru och Nwoya i norra Uganda; Yumbe, Adjumani, Arua och Moyo i West Nile; Moroto, Nakapiripit, Kaabong och Amudat i Karamoja; Kasese, Buliisa och Hoima i västra Uganda/Rwenzori-regionen. De primära kriterierna för valet av de 14 distrikten är förekomsten av flera sammanlänkade och ej hanterade konfliktorsaker.

The overall goal of the programme is to contribute to more peaceful, secure and resilient communities in Uganda. At the outcome level, it is hoped that communities, formal and informal authorities and civil society in target locations, work together across conflict divides to build peace and resolve conflicts. This programme is rooted in Saferworld’s organisational change model, which identifies three essential conditions for peace:1) That people play an active role in preventing and transforming conflict and building peace; 2) That people with influence use their power to promote inclusive, just and equitable societies.3) That people have access to fair and effective paths to address the grievances and inequalities that drive conflict Therefore to achieve the overall programme goal, Saferworld will focus on three outcomes organised by the actor categories namely, communities, formal and informal authorities and Civil Society Organisations. Saferworld will work with and influence these actors to address underlying drivers of conflict and insecurity. The outcome areas are; Outcome 1: Communities (including women, youth, refugees, hosts and other marginalized groups) at risk of- and/or affected by conflict in at least 14 districts identify, prioritise, analyse, monitor and take coordinated action to respond to local conflict issues and their root causes, through existing and/or new community peace building structures. Outcome 2: Formal and informal authorities responsible for building peace, security and justice at local, district and national levels, consult more with communities on identified conflict issues, support community peace building structures in responding to conflict issues, and incorporate community concerns (including issues affecting marginalized groups) into their related responses. Outcome 3: CSOs work together to influence relevant peace, security and justice processes and decision-making at district/regional and national levels, including donors and private sector, connecting them to communities’ concerns and priorities; and to incorporate conflict sensitive practices into their activities and programmes

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
The programme aimed at addressing four conflict drivers namely; natural resources including land, refugee influx, inadequate transitional justice processes and volatile electoral processes. The Programme activity implementation period came to an end in December 2023. In May 2024, Saferworld submitted a final project narrative report and an End Term Evaluation report. The reports shows that several results were achieved during the project period (1 January 2021 to 31 December 2023) as elaborated below.
Outcome 1: Communities at risk of- and/or affected by conflict in at least 14 districts identify, prioritise, analyse, monitor and take coordinated action to respond to local conflict issues through community peace building structures.
Identification and resolution of conflicts; During programme implementation, Saferworld established 56 Community Action Groups (CAGs) and Community Based Therapy groups (CBTs). The CAGS are a mechanism through which Saferworld and TPO supported communities with trainings, technical assistance and financial support. The Community Action Groups were empowered to identify, monitor and take action on conflicts while the CBTs were used to provide psycho-social support.
Community Action Groups were able to resolve conflicts in the four regions of Northern, Western, West Nile and Karamoja. Majority of the conflicts that were resolved related to natural resources (primarily land conflicts ) including those related to human wildlife conflicts and refugee communities. For example; In West Nile, the CAGS began dialogues between communities and district leaders. They identified conflicts arising out of the high demand for farmland by the refugees. Following the recommendations from the dialogues, Saferworld partner organisation conducted a scoping study in December 2022 on access to alternative land for refugees for farming to inform advocacy interventions for food secure and resilient refugee communities in Uganda. The findings were shared with community members and relevant district authorities through a series of engagements. As a result, in May 2023, the host communities released land totalling 2,125 acres to the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) and local government. Refugee households were allocated plots for farming by the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM). This reduced land disputes, increased production and promoted peaceful co-existence between refugees and the host community in West Nile.
In Karamoja sub-region, two communities agreed on resource sharing for joint grazing and access to water as a result of the peace dialogues held between the conflicting communities by CAGS, informal leaders, security forces and the Area Land Committees. This has enhanced peace, trade, free movement, shared pasture resources and water sources. The communities have reported reduction in cases of cattle theft and road attacks and there is free movement of people.
Additionally, Saferworld conducted a meeting with Artisanal and Small-Scale Miners Association to document their plight. The meeting revealed a lot of challenges that miners go through including exploitation by investors and poor working conditions. The proceedings were used to engage the district local government and CSOs to advocate for the rights of the miners. The district local government together with CSOs and miners' leaders held a series of engagements and the prices of Mable stones have been increased from 60,000 to 120,000 UGX. This has improved household income and reduced conflicts and the sub-county officials are now supervising and monitoring the operations in the mines.
Enhancing awareness on processes and procedures on land tenure; Most land in the communities is held communally and communities were not aware of the processes and procedures of seeking for security of tenure. As a result, some family or community members would sell land without the involvement of the other members of the family leading to conflicts. CAGs conducted awareness sessions on land acquisition and management procedures in the community with support from area land committees and local leaders. Community members gained knowledge on how to demarcate their land, acquire customary certificates and ways to resolve conflicts peaceful. Evidence to support this change is the presence of registration forms at the sub-county as well as testimonies from community members. In Western Uganda, community members were able to obtain a caveat on land that was illegally sold to a private individual outside of the community without community consultation.
Enhancing the role of women in peace processes - In the four regions of Northern, Western, West Nile and Karamoja where the project was implemented, women were empowered through trainings in conflict prevention, peace building, GBV and MHPSS. As a result, women contributed to peace processes at family, community, district levels and making recommendations in conflict prevention and peace building as this is considered a male space. They led on raising awareness on the dangers of GBV including forming anti-GBV clubs in schools, formal land acquisition and dispute resolution including written land transaction agreements, which has reduced on cases of multiple land ownership conflicts, and improved social relations, and peaceful co-existence in the four regions. Historically, cultural norms in these regions limit women's participation in conflict prevention, peace-building, and unresolved concerns.
Improved mental health and livelihoods; The programme created 34 Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Groups(CBT) of 408 individuals through which Mental and Psycho-social support was provided. The individuals were taken through 10-week CBT therapy that restored their hope and positive outlook on life. Following graduation of the groups and post assessment, livelihood assessment was conducted with all the groups to ascertain their livelihood needs which informed the disbursement of funds to the groups for establishment of selected income generating activities. As a result, different projects/enterprises started in the different regions. The groups are now actively involved in productive activities like farming and selling farm produce. A few groups have managed to make profit in the past months. This has created better socio-economic well-being since people are engaged in business ventures. It has also improved social cohesion since members are working as a group and has also enabled members benefit from Government and other CSO economic enterprises.
Outcome 2: Formal and informal authorities responsible for building peace, security, justice and psychosocial healing at local, district and national levels, consult more with communities on identified conflict issues, support community peace building structures in responding to conflict issues, and incorporate community concerns into their related responses.
The programme enhanced relationships between authorities and communities. This was evidenced by how authorities started responding to community concerns. In Karamoja region, following dialogues with Community Action Groups, Uganda Wild Life Authority (UWA) allowed local communities to have access to traditional shrines and collect natural resources from the national park in Karenga district. UWA also allocated rangers to protect the food basket in Nampaya farmland following reports about wild animals destroying food crops in the area. In Western Uganda, the local government and UWA are responding to community out cry on human- wildlife conflict by supporting the construction of an electric fence along the boundary of Murchison Falls National park and recruiting scouts to support in surveillance and deterrence of stray animals.
Saferworld supported the Yumbe and Moyo District local governments in facilitating a dialogue that resolved a community land boundary conflict that erupted in May 2023 between the Kuku people of South Sudan and the Aringa people of Yumbe district. The conflict had displaced over 3,000 people, destroyed 420 houses and caused the disappearance of over 100 cattle. Saferworld engaged OPM and district local authorities over the matter. After the two districts agreeing to resolve the matter through dialogues, Saferworld provided funds to facilitate the meeting between district officials and South Sudan officials. The resolutions passed from the dialogue enabled the displaced communities to return to the contested land.
During programme implementation, Saferworld supported several districts to develop and operationalise Conflict and Gender Sensitive Investment Policies (CGSIP).The vision of the policy is a vibrant and competitive local economy applying conflict sensitive productivity enhancing environment friendly technologies for poverty reduction, wealth creation and prosperity. Following the development of the policies, Moroto district government authorities together with Community Action groups facilitated a meeting between investors at rata mining site and the workers given complaints of late payment and working without protective wear. Following the dialogue, investors started paying workers timely and providing adequate protective gears leading to improved relations within the mining site.
In West Nile, the authorities especially the justice service providers have started working in a complimentary manner while responding to community concerns. This has increased trust in the local court justice systems. Local council courts have now dedicated two days per week to settle civil disputes in the community.
By the end of the programme, there was an improvement in health seeking behaviour for mental health cases within the community as the people seeking treatment at health facility and positive attitude towards mental health at community and health facility level increased. This also improved the well-being of clients and reduced GBV cases at family level. During programme implementation, Saferworld and TPO organised trainings for health workers on Mental health Gap Action Program (MhGAP). Following the trainings, health workers in Western and Northern Uganda were able to screen, identify and refer mental health clients to government hospitals. Health workers also passed on information on mental health to community members, screened, treated and referred mental cases. The ripple effect has been the transmission of the knowledge acquired to their fellow workers and using platforms such as places of worship and community outreach to raise awareness on mental health.
Outcome 3: CSOs work together to influence relevant peace, security and justice processes and decision making at district/regional and national levels.
Following the establishment and support for Civil Society Platforms, CSOs started working together to support peace building activities. In Karamoja, CSOs developed a Civil Military Cooperation (CIMIC) guide, and this has improved relations, engagement and coordination between CSOs and the military on disarmament and peace building activities. In Western Uganda, following research done by a regional partner, Rwenzori Information Centre Network (RICNET) on human-wildlife conflicts in Western Uganda, an issue paper was developed and presented by the Member of Parliament of Busongora North on the floor of parliament in April 2023. The house thereafter tasked the Minister for Tourism, Wildlife and Antiquities to ensure electric fences are installed and to also look into other mechanisms to counter the problem.
Through the community dialogues conducted by CAGS and CBT groups, the project contributed to a number of unforeseen positive outcomes including, reduced alcohol abuse, reduced stigma on mental health, decreased incidences of domestic violence, increased school retention rates and enhanced skills and capacities of community members. In one sub-county, teenage pregnancy reduced by about 50% among the students in host communities. 5 teenage mothers were returned to school by their parents and two girls were rescued from early marriages and returned to school. Six young men that were using marijuana were enrolled into vocational school and successfully completed their studies. There has been a reported increase in enrolment of children in school at the beginning of the 2023 academic year compared to 2022 as a result of sensitisation and awareness creation of the community members. While these outcomes do not directly relate to the four conflict drivers, they address what could be triggers or consequences of conflicts.
Another unforeseen outcome is that the project empowered community members particularly those involved in mediating and identifying conflict which has resulted in them acquiring jobs and taking up leadership roles in the communities. At the the end of the programme, Saferworld reported that 12 percent of them had been absorbed by districts authorities as para-social workers, women councilors, chairpersons and members of Area Land Committees among other leadership positions in their sub counties. Others found gainful employment, with Civil Society Organisations and companies such as Total Energies. A number of them indicated that they are preparing to stand for leadership positions in the 2026 general elections.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
